Fountains Abbey is a ruined Cistercian monastery near Ripon in North Yorkshire, England. It was founded in 1132 under the direction of Thurstan, archbishop of York, and over the next four centuries became one of the wealthiest monasteries in England thanks to its large and diverse landholdings. The monastery was dissolved in 1539 as part of the English Reformation and its estates sold. Fountains Abbey is now within Studley Royal Park, a landscaped garden created in the eighteenth century.
Even in its current state, Fountains is described by Historic England as "the best preserved of English abbeys and [...] the finest picturesque ruin." The majority of the buildings were constructed in the Romanesque and Early English Gothic style between 1170 and 1247, with significant additions in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. It also forms part of the Studley Royal including the ruins of Fountains Abbey World Heritage Site. It is owned by the National Trust and maintained by English Heritage, and is open to the public.

'''Fountains Abbey''' is a ruined [[Cistercians|Cistercian]] monastery near [[Ripon]] in [[North Yorkshire]], England. It was founded in 1132 under the direction of [[Thurstan]], [[archbishop of York]], and over the next four centuries became one of the wealthiest monasteries in England thanks to its large and diverse landholdings. The monastery was [[Dissolution of the monasteries|dissolved]] in 1539 as part of the [[English Reformation]] and its estates sold. Fountains Abbey is now within [[Studley Royal Park]], a [[English landscape garden|landscaped garden]] created in the eighteenth century.

Even in its current state, Fountains is described by [[Historic England]] as "the best preserved of English [[abbey]]s and [...] the finest picturesque ruin." The majority of the buildings were constructed in the [[Romanesque architecture|Romanesque]] and [[Early English Gothic]] style between 1170 and 1247, with significant additions in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. The abbey church and many of the [[claustral]] buildings survive, including the [[chapter house]], [[refectory]], and [[lay brother]]s' dormitory, as well as ancillary structures such as the guest houses, [[Fountains Mill|abbey mill]], and bridges.

The abbey is protected for its historic significance, having been designated a [[grade I listed building]] and a [[scheduled monument]] by Historic England. It also forms part of the ''Studley Royal including the ruins of Fountains Abbey'' [[World Heritage Site]]. It is owned by the [[National Trust]] and maintained by [[English Heritage]], and is open to the public.

==Foundation==
After a dispute and riot in 1132 at the [[Benedictine]] house of [[St Mary's Abbey, York]], thirteen monks were expelled, among them [[Robert of Newminster]], who was later [[canonised]]. They were taken under the protection of [[Thurstan]], [[Archbishop of York]],<ref>{{harvnb|Coppack|1993|page=17}}</ref> who provided them with land in the valley of the [[River Skell]], a tributary of the [[River Ure|Ure]]. The enclosed valley had all the natural features needed for the creation of a monastery, providing shelter from the weather; stone and timber for building; and a supply of running water.<ref name="History of the Abbey">{{cite web|url=http://www.fountainsabbey.org.uk/html/visiting/what-to-see/the-abbey/ |title= The Abbey |publisher=The National Trust |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080914061614/http://www.fountainsabbey.org.uk/html/visiting/what-to-see/the-abbey/ |archive-date=14 September 2008 |work=Fountains Abbey and Studley Royal}}</ref> The six springs that watered the site inspired the monks to give it the name of Fountains.<ref>{{cite book |last=Mills |first=A. D. |date=2011 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tXucAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA193 |title=A Dictionary of British Place Names |publisher=Oxford University Press |page=193 |isbn=978-0-19-107894-1}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |editor-last=Hourihane |editor-first=Colum |date=2012 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FtlMAgAAQBAJ&pg=RA1-PA552 |title=The Grove Encyclopedia of Medieval Art and Architecture |chapter=Fountains Abbey |volume=2 |page=552 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-539536-5}}</ref>

After enduring a harsh winter in 1133, the monks applied to join the [[Cistercians|Cistercian]] order, which since the end of the previous century had been a fast-growing reform movement and by the beginning of the 13th century had more than 500 houses. In 1135 Fountains became the second Cistercian house in northern England, after [[Rievaulx Abbey]]. The monks of Fountains became subject to [[Clairvaux Abbey]] in [[Duchy of Burgundy|Burgundy]], which was under the rule of [[Bernard of Clairvaux|St Bernard]]. Under the guidance of Geoffrey of Ainai, a monk sent from Clairvaux, the group learned how to celebrate the seven [[Canonical Hours|canonical hours]] according to Cistercian usage and were shown how to construct wooden buildings in accordance with [[Cistercian architecture|Cistercian practice]].<ref>{{cite book|editor-first=Brian Patrick |editor-last=McGuire |title=A Companion to Bernard of Clairvaux|publisher= Brill, Leiden|year= 2011 |page= 198}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url= http://cistercians.shef.ac.uk/fountains/history/foundation/ |title= Foundation: a Cistercian identity |access-date=5 February 2012}}</ref><ref name="vch">[https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/yorks/vol3/pp134-138 Hisotry of the County of York, Volume 3]: Houses of Cistercian monks: Fountains</ref>

==Consolidation==
According to archaeologist Glyn Coppack, after [[Henry Murdac]] was elected abbot in 1143 the small stone church and timber [[Cloister|claustral]] buildings were replaced; the new church was similar in plan to the church at [[Vauclair Abbey]] that Murdac had previously commissioned.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Keevill |first1=Graham |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=f9KHDgAAQBAJ&dq=henry+murdac&pg=PA175 |title=Monastic Archaeology |last2=Aston |first2=Mick |last3=Hall |first3=Teresa |date=31 January 2017 |publisher=OXBOW Books |isbn=978-1-78570-570-0 |pages=178 }}</ref> Within three years an aisled nave had been added to the stone church, and the first permanent claustral buildings, built in stone and roofed in tile, had been completed.<ref>{{harvnb|Coppack|2009|page=34}}</ref>

In 1146 an angry mob, annoyed at Murdac because of his role in opposing the election of [[William of York|William FitzHerbert]] as [[archbishop of York]], attacked the abbey and burned down all but the church and some surrounding buildings.<ref>{{harvnb|Coppack|1993|pages=32–33}}</ref> The community recovered swiftly from the attack and founded four daughter houses. Henry Murdac resigned as abbot in 1147 upon becoming archbishop of York.<ref>{{cite book |last=Spigelman |first=James J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3FHwzF_hmUYC&dq=henry+murdac&pg=PA28 |title=Becket & Henry: The Becket Lectures |date=2004 |publisher=James Spigelman |isbn=978-0-646-43477-3 |pages=28 }}</ref> He was replaced first by Maurice, abbot of Rievaulx (1147–8), then, on the resignation of Maurice, by Thorald (1148–50). Thorald was forced by Murdac, now archbishop, to resign after two years in office.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Powicke |first=F. M. |date=1921 |title=Maurice of Rievaulx |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/552640 |journal=The English Historical Review |volume=36 |issue=141 |pages=17–29 |doi=10.1093/ehr/XXXVI.CXLI.17 |jstor=552640 |issn=0013-8266}}</ref>

The next abbot, Richard, restored the abbey's stability and prosperity. During his twenty years as abbot he supervised an extensive building programme that involved completing repairs to the damaged church and building more accommodation for the increasing number of recruits. At his death in 1170 the chapter house was complete and the new church almost finished.<ref>{{cite ODNB |title=Richard [Richard of Fountains] (d. 1170), abbot of Fountains |url=https://www.oxforddnb.com/view/10.1093/ref:odnb/9780198614128.001.0001/odnb-9780198614128-e-23510 |access-date=7 July 2022 | year=2004 |doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/23510| isbn=978-0-19-861412-8 }}</ref> The work was continued by his successor, Robert of Pipewell.<ref>{{cite web |title=St Mary of Fountains, Fountains Abbey: 01. Church and general material |url=https://www.crsbi.ac.uk/view-item?i=2289 |access-date=7 July 2022 |website=CRSBI }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |first1=Julie |last1=Kerr |first2=Sarah |last2=Foot |title=Robert of Pipewell |url=https://www.dhi.ac.uk/cistercians/people/robert-of-pipewell.php |access-date=7 July 2022 |website=www.dhi.ac.uk }}</ref> 

The next abbot was William of Newminster, a noted [[Asceticism|ascetic]], who presided over the abbey from 1180 to 1190.<ref>{{cite web |first1=Julie |last1=Kerr |first2=Sarah |last2=Foot |title=William of Newminster, abbot of Fountains 1180-90 |url=https://www.dhi.ac.uk/cistercians/people/wm-newminster.php |access-date=7 July 2022 |website=www.dhi.ac.uk }}</ref> He was succeeded by Ralph Haget, who had entered Fountains at the age of 30 as a novice after pursuing a military career.<ref name=":0">{{cite book |last=France |first=James |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=X76At6xzA7MC&dq=ralph+haget&pg=PR22 |title=Separate but Equal: Cistercian Lay Brothers 1120-1350 |date=1 December 2012 |publisher=Liturgical Press |isbn=978-0-87907-747-1 |pages=14, 178 }}</ref> Prior to his abbacy at Fountains, from 1182 to 1190/1 he was abbot of [[Kirkstall Abbey]].<ref name=":0" /> During the European famine of 1194 the abbey provided support for six months to local people in the form of food, shelter and spiritual care.<ref>{{cite book |last=Kerr |first=Julie |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UlwJBAAAQBAJ&dq=famine+1194+fountains+abbey&pg=PA36 |title=Life in the Medieval Cloister |date=14 May 2009 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |isbn=978-1-4411-2509-5 |pages=36 }}</ref> Famine was joined by the spread of disease, and the abbey helped those who needed treatment.<ref name=":1">{{cite book |last=Knowles |first=David |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rn-TJNOBGlQC&dq=famine+1194+fountains+abbey&pg=PA358 |title=The Monastic Order in England: A History of Its Development from the Times of St Dunstan to the Fourth Lateran Council 940-1216 |date=29 January 2004 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-54808-3 |pages=358 }}</ref> During the first half of the 13th century Fountains increased in reputation and prosperity under John of York (1203–1211),<ref name=":2">{{cite web |title=Houses of Cistercian monks: Fountains {{!}} British History Online |url=https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/yorks/vol3/pp134-138 |access-date=7 July 2022 |website=www.british-history.ac.uk}}</ref> John of Hessle (1211–1220)<ref>{{cite book |last=Robinson |first=David Martin |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DShUAAAAMAAJ&q=john+of+hessle+1211+-+1220 |title=The Cistercian Abbeys of Britain: Far from the Concourse of Men |date=1998 |publisher=B.T. Batsford |isbn=978-0-7134-8392-5 |pages=115}}</ref> and John of Kent (1220–1247).<ref name=":2" /> These three abbots managed to complete another expansion of the abbey's buildings, which included enlarging the church and building an infirmary.<ref name=":1" />

==Difficulties==
During the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries, the north of England was subject to increased taxation, Fountains Abbey included. According to [[William Grainge]], writing in ''Annals of a Yorkshire Abbey: A Popular History of the Famous Monastery of Fountains,'' the taxation of temporal goods had reduced from £343 in 1292, to £243 in 1318. Grainge interprets this reduction as evidence for detriment to the estate of the abbey. The abbey was criticised for its dire material and physical state when it was visited by Archbishop [[John le Romeyn]] in 1294,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Cassidy-Welch |first=Megan |date=1 January 2001 |title=Incarceration and Liberation: Prisons in the Cistercian Monastery |url=https://www.brepolsonline.net/doi/10.1484/J.VIATOR.2.300728 |journal=Viator |volume=32 |pages=23–42 |doi=10.1484/J.VIATOR.2.300728 |issn=0083-5897 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> and by the 1330s was no longer working to surplus, but having to borrow money.<ref name=":8">{{cite book |last1=Grainge |first1=William |url=https://www.irhb.org/wiki/index.php/Grainge,_William_1880a |title=Annals of a Yorkshire Abbey: A Popular History of the Famous Monastery of Fountains, from its Foundation to the Present Time; the Excavations made and Relics found at Different Periods; with a Survey & Description of the Ruins |date=1880 |publisher=[[Robert Ackrill]] |location=Harrogate, England |pages=27, 34, 56 |access-date=18 April 2021}}</ref>

By the second half of the 13th century the abbey was in working in straitened circumstances. It was presided over by eleven abbots, and became financially unstable largely due to [[Forward contract|forward selling]] its wool crop.<ref>{{cite book |last=Knowles |first=David |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9BjEJcCKyFAC&dq=fountains+abbey+forward+selling&pg=PA68 |title=Religious Orders Vol 1 |date=27 September 1979 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-29566-6 |pages=68–9 }}</ref> The run of disasters that befell the community continued into the early 14th century when northern England was invaded by the Scots and there were further demands for taxes. The culmination of these misfortunes was the [[Black Death]] of 1348–1349. The loss of manpower and income due to the ravages of the plague was almost ruinous.<ref>{{cite book |last=Newsome |first=Clive |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Syg8cN9n6XgC&dq=fountains+abbey+black+death&pg=PA53 |title=The Abbey Trail |date=2003 |publisher=SIGMA PRESS |isbn=978-1-85058-803-0 |pages=53 }}</ref><ref name=":5" />

A further complication arose as a result of the [[Papal Schism of 1378]]–1409. Fountains and other English Cistercian houses were told to break off contact with the mother house of Citeaux, which supported a rival pope. This resulted in the abbots forming their own chapter to rule the order in England, and they became increasingly involved in internecine politics.<ref name=":5">{{cite book |last1=Burton |first1=Janet |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=adHIaVe-zBgC&dq=fountains+abbey+papal+schism+1378&pg=PA99 |title=The Cistercians in the Middle Ages |last2=Burton |first2=Janet E. |last3=Kerr |first3=Julie |date=2011 |publisher=Boydell Press |isbn=978-1-84383-667-4 |pages=99–100, 176 }}</ref> In 1410, following the death of Abbot Burley of Fountains, the community was riven by several years of turmoil over the election of his successor. John Ripon, abbot of Meaux, and Roger Frank, a monk of Fountains, were locked in conflict until 1416 when Ripon was finally appointed, ruling until his death in 1434.<ref>{{cite ODNB |title=Ripon, John (d. 1435), abbot of Fountains |url=https://www.oxforddnb.com/view/10.1093/ref:odnb/9780198614128.001.0001/odnb-9780198614128-e-107118 |access-date=7 July 2022 |year=2004 |doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/107118|isbn=978-0-19-861412-8 }}</ref>
[[File:Fountains_Abbey_(3998296735).jpg|thumb|Fountains Abbey - Huby's Tower]]
Fountains regained some stability and prosperity under abbots [[Poisoning of Abbot John Greenwell|John Greenwell]] (1442–1471),<ref name=":3">{{cite ODNB |title=Greenwell, John (d. in or after 1471), abbot of Fountains |url=https://www.oxforddnb.com/view/10.1093/ref:odnb/9780198614128.001.0001/odnb-9780198614128-e-107119 |access-date=7 July 2022 |year=2015 |doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/107119|isbn=978-0-19-861412-8 |last1=Walker |first1=John }}</ref> Thomas Swinton (1471–1478),<ref name=":4">{{cite web |first1=Julie |last1=Kerr |first2=Sarah |last2=Foot |title=Thomas Swinton, abbot of Fountains, 1471-78 (resigned) |url=https://www.dhi.ac.uk/cistercians/people/thomas-swinton.php |access-date=7 July 2022 |website=www.dhi.ac.uk }}</ref> and John Darnton (1478–1495),<ref>{{cite web |first1=Julie |last1=Kerr |first2=Sarah |last2=Foot |title=John Darnton, abbot of Fountains, 1479-95 |url=https://www.dhi.ac.uk/cistercians/people/john-darnton.php |access-date=7 July 2022 |website=www.dhi.ac.uk }}</ref> who undertook some much needed restoration of the fabric of the abbey, including notable work on the church. During Greenwell's abbacy, he reduced the debts of the abbey by 1000 marks, and survived [[Poisoning of Abbot Greenwell|a poisoning attempt]] by a monk called William Downom.<ref name=":3" /> Swinton kept a detailed "Memorandum Book", which provides exceptional detail on the life of the abbey during his abbacy.<ref name=":4" /> Marmaduke Huby (1495–1526) expanded the number of monks from twenty-two to fifty-two and undertook a building programme which included an extension to the infirmary and a new tower attached to the north transept.<ref>{{cite ODNB |title=Huby, Marmaduke (c. 1439–1526), abbot of Fountains |url=https://www.oxforddnb.com/view/10.1093/ref:odnb/9780198614128.001.0001/odnb-9780198614128-e-53115 |access-date=7 July 2022 | year=2004 |doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/53115| isbn=978-0-19-861412-8 }}</ref> Huby's Tower, as it became known, is decorated with the abbot's insignia, as well as religious texts.<ref name=":6">{{cite journal |last=Carter |first=Michael |date=1 June 2010 |title=The Tower of Abbot Marmaduke Huby of Fountains Abbey: Hubris or Piety? |url=https://doi.org/10.1179/yaj.2010.82.1.269 |journal=Yorkshire Archaeological Journal |volume=82 |issue=1 |pages=269–286 |doi=10.1179/yaj.2010.82.1.269 |s2cid=191329280 |issn=0084-4276|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

At Abbot Huby's death he was succeeded by William Thirsk, who was accused by the royal commissioners of immorality and inadequacy and dismissed as abbot, retiring to [[Jervaulx Abbey]]; he was later hanged for his involvement in the [[Pilgrimage of Grace]].<ref>{{cite web |first1=Julie |last1=Kerr |first2=Sarah |last2=Foot |title=William Thirsk, abbot of Fountains |url=https://www.dhi.ac.uk/cistercians/people/wm-thirsk.php |access-date=7 July 2022 |website=www.dhi.ac.uk }}</ref> He was replaced by Marmaduke Bradley, a monk of the abbey who had reported Thirsk's supposed offences and testified against him.<ref name=":9" /> Furthermore, Bradley paid 600 marks to essentially buy the abbacy for himself.<ref>{{harvnb|Coppack|2009|pages=128}}</ref> In 1539 it was Bradley who surrendered the abbey when its seizure was ordered under [[Henry VIII]] at the [[dissolution of the monasteries]].<ref name=":9">{{cite web |first1=Julie |last1=Kerr |first2=Sarah |last2=Foot |title=Marmaduke Bradley |url=https://www.dhi.ac.uk/cistercians/people/marmaduke-bradley.php |access-date=7 July 2022 |website=www.dhi.ac.uk }}</ref>

==Architecture==

[[File:Fountains Abbey 2016 124.jpg|thumb|upright=1.55|left|Interior of the abbey church looking down the nave]]

The abbey precinct covered {{convert|70|acre|ha}} surrounded by an {{convert|11|ft|m|adj=on}} wall built in the 13th century, some parts of which are visible to the south and west of the abbey. The area consists of three concentric zones cut by the River Skell flowing from west to east across the site. The church and claustral buildings stand at the centre of the precinct north of the Skell. The inner court containing the domestic buildings stretches down to the river and the outer court housing the industrial and agricultural buildings lies on the river's south bank. The early abbey buildings were added to and altered over time, resulting in deviations from the strict Cistercian type. Outside the walls were the abbey's "home [[Monastic grange|grange]]s".<ref>{{harvnb|Coppack|2009|pages=115–7}}</ref>

The original abbey church was built of wood and "was probably" two storeys high; it was, however, quickly replaced in stone. The church was damaged in the attack on the abbey in 1146 and was rebuilt, in a larger scale, on the same site. Building work was completed {{circa|1170}}.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://cistercians.shef.ac.uk/fountains/buildings/church/church2.php|title= The Abbey Church |access-date=6 February 2012}}</ref> This structure, completed around 1170, was {{convert|300|ft|m|abbr=on}} long and had 11 bays in the side aisles. A [[lantern tower]] was added at the crossing of the church in the late 12th century. The presbytery at the eastern end of the church was much altered in the 13th century.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://cistercians.shef.ac.uk/fountains/buildings/church/church3.php |title= The layout of the Church |access-date=6 February 2012}}</ref> The church's greatly lengthened choir, commenced by Abbot John of York, 1203–11 and carried on by his successor, terminates, like that of [[Durham Cathedral]], in an eastern transept, the work of Abbot John of Kent, 1220–47.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Cothren |first=Michael |date=1 January 1982 |title=Cistercian Tile Mosaic Pavements In Yorkshire: Context And Sources |url=https://works.swarthmore.edu/fac-art/115 |journal=Studies in Cistercian Art and Architecture |volume=1}}</ref> Similarities to the choir at [[Beverley Minster]] have been drawn by architectural historian Lawrence Hoey.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Hoey |first=Lawrence |date=1984 |title=Beverley Minster in Its 13th-Century Context |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/990002 |journal=Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians |volume=43 |issue=3 |pages=209–224 |doi=10.2307/990002 |jstor=990002 |issn=0037-9808|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The {{convert|160|ft|m|adj=mid|-tall}} tower, which was added not long before the dissolution, by Abbot Huby, 1494–1526, is in an unusual position at the northern end of the north transept and bears Huby's motto: ''Soli Deo Honor et Gloria (Honor and Glory to God Alone)''.<ref name=":6" /> The [[sacristry]] adjoined the south transept.<ref>{{cite web |title=Sacristy – The Cistercians in Yorkshire |url=https://www.dhi.ac.uk/blogs/cistercians/fountains-abbey/buildings/sacristy/ |access-date=7 July 2022 }}</ref>

The [[cloister]], which had arcading of black marble from Nidderdale and white sandstone, is in the centre of the precinct and to the south of the church. The three-aisled [[chapter-house]] and parlour open from the eastern walk of the cloister, with the monks' dormitory above; along the cloister's southern walk are, from east to west, the [[calefactory|warming house]] with muniment room above, the refectory, and the kitchens. Parallel with the western walk is an immense, vaulted substructure known as the cellarium (divided into sections serving as cellars and store-rooms, and with the lay brothers' refectory at its southern end, next to the kitchens), which supported the [[dormitory]] of the ''conversi'' ([[lay brother]]s) above. This building extended across the river and at its south-west corner were the [[Reredorter|latrines]], built above the swiftly flowing stream.<ref>{{harvnb|Coppack|2009|pages=63–70}}</ref>

{{wide image|Fountains_Abbey_view_crop1_2005-08-27.jpg|950px|align-cap=center|View of Fountains Abbey looking from west to south}}

The infirmary is located to the east of the latrine block, where portions of it are suspended on arches over the River Skell. It was built in the mid-12th century as a modest single-storey structure, then, from the 14th century, underwent extensive expansion and remodelling to end up in the 16th century as a grand dwelling with fine bay windows and large fireplaces. The great hall was an expansive room {{convert|52|by|21|m|ft|order=flip}},<ref name=Colliers/> "one of the largest aisled halls ever built in mediaeval England".<ref>{{harvnb|Coppack|2009|page=80}}</ref> The infirmary had its own oratory or chapel, {{convert|46+1/2|by|23|ft|m|0|adj=on}}, and a kitchen, {{convert|50|by|38|ft|m|adj=on}}.

To the west of the cloister was the lay brothers' infirmary, and beyond that the two guest houses still visible, and a large guest hall to the north of them. Only the base of a pier and a table leg survive of the guest hall, but its plan has been established by geophysical survey.<ref>{{harvnb|Coppack|2009|page=72}}</ref>

To the east of the abbey, north of the infirmary, is the monks' cemetery. It was long known to exist, but its extent and arrangement were only discovered in 2016, when a partnership between the National Trust, the [[University of Bradford]], Geoscan Research, Magnitude Surveys and Guideline Geo used ground penetrating radar which discovered several hundred graves in a careful and orderly arrangement.<ref>{{cite news

==Endowments and economy==
Medieval monasteries were sustained by [[Estate (land)|landed estates]] that were given to them as endowments and from which they derived an income from rents. They were the gifts of the founder and subsequent patrons, but some were purchased from cash revenues. At the outset, the Cistercian order rejected gifts of mills and rents, churches with [[tithes]] and [[Feudalism|feudal]] manors as they did not accord with their belief in monastic purity, because they involved contact with laymen. When Archbishop Thurstan founded the abbey he gave the community {{convert|260|acre|ha}} of land at [[Sutton Grange, North Yorkshire|Sutton]] north of the abbey and {{convert|200|acre|ha}} at Herleshowe to provide support while the abbey became established. In the early years the abbey struggled to maintain itself because further gifts were not forthcoming. Thurstan could not help further because the lands he administered were not his own, but part of the diocesan estate. After several years of impoverished struggle to establish the abbey, the monks were joined by Hugh, a former dean of [[York Minster]], a rich man who brought a considerable fortune as well as furniture and books to start the library.<ref name="vch"/>

By 1135 the monks had acquired only another {{convert|260|acre|ha}} at [[South Stainley|Cayton]], given by Eustace fitzJohn of Knaresborough "for the building of the abbey". Shortly after the fire of 1146, the monks had established [[Monastic grange|granges]] at Sutton, Cayton, [[Cowton Moor]], [[Warsill]], [[Dacre, North Yorkshire|Dacre]] and [[Aldborough, North Yorkshire|Aldburgh]]<ref>{{harvnb|Coppack|2005|page=97}}</ref> all within {{convert|6|mi|km|0|abbr=on}} of Fountains. In the 1140s the water mill was built on the abbey site, so that the grain from the granges could be brought to the abbey for milling.<ref>{{harvnb|Coppack|2005|page=99}}</ref>

In October 2021, the National Trust announced that they had uncovered the foundations of a 12th- to 13th-century [[tannery]] at the abbey, described as being of "industrial" scale. The foundations, located close to the River Skell, were discovered using ground-penetrating radar, revealing a number of previously-unknown monastic buildings along a long, "bowling alley-type extension" whose use had long been unknown.<ref name="guardian 2021">{{cite web |last=Brown |first=Mark |date=25 October 2021 |title=Archaeologists find 'missing link' in history of Fountains Abbey |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2021/oct/25/archaeologists-find-missing-link-history-fountains-abbey |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20211025121957/https://www.theguardian.com/science/2021/oct/25/archaeologists-find-missing-link-history-fountains-abbey |archive-date=25 October 2021 |access-date=25 October 2021 |work=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref>

Further estates were assembled in two phases, between 1140 and 1160 then 1174 and 1175, from piecemeal acquisitions of land. Some of the lands were grants from benefactors but others were purchased from gifts of money to the abbey. Roger de Mowbray granted large areas of [[Nidderdale]] and William de Percy and his tenants granted substantial estates in [[Craven in the Domesday Book|Craven]] which included [[Malham Moor]] and the fishery in [[Malham Tarn]].<ref>{{harvnb|Coppack|2003|page=108}}</ref> After 1203 the abbots consolidated the abbey's lands by renting out more distant areas that the monks could not easily farm themselves, and exchanging and purchasing lands that complemented their existing estates. Fountains' holdings both in [[Yorkshire]] and beyond had reached their maximum extent by 1265, when they were an efficient and very profitable estate. Their estates were linked in a network of individual granges which provided staging posts to the most distant ones. They had urban properties in York, [[Yarm]], [[Grimsby]], [[Scarborough, North Yorkshire|Scarborough]] and [[Boston, Lincolnshire|Boston]] from which to conduct export and market trading and their other commercial interests included mining, quarrying, iron-smelting, fishing and milling.<ref>{{harvnb|Coppack|2003|pages=111–114}}</ref>

Apart from the renting out of land, the monks themselves and their laybrothers, numerous in the early period, were committed on a large scale to its efficient development and the management of the landscape, not least the watercourses and woods.

The [[Battle of Bannockburn]] in 1314 was a factor that led to a downturn in the prosperity of the abbey in the early fourteenth century. Areas of the north of England as far south as York were looted by the Scots. Then the number of lay-brothers being recruited to the order reduced considerably. The abbey chose to take advantage of the relaxation of the edict on leasing property that had been enacted by the General Chapter of the order in 1208 and leased some of their properties. Others were staffed by hired labour and remained in hand under the supervision of bailiffs. In 1535 Fountains had an interest in 138 [[vill]]s and the total taxable income of the Fountains estate was £1,115, making it the richest Cistercian monastery in England.<ref>{{harvnb|Coppack|2003|page=104}}</ref>

==After the Dissolution==
[[Image:Grasshopper-crest.GIF|thumb|105px|Gresham family crest|alt=]]
The Abbey buildings and land were seized by the Crown, and sold on 1 October 1540 to Sir [[Richard Gresham]], at the time a [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|Member of Parliament]] (MP) and previously [[List of Lord Mayors of London|Lord Mayor]] of [[City of London|London]], the father of Sir [[Thomas Gresham]]. It was Richard Gresham who had supplied [[Cardinal Wolsey]] with the tapestries for his new residence of [[Hampton Court]] and who paid for the Cardinal's funeral.<ref>{{cite web |title=GRESHAM, Sir Richard (by 1486-1549), of London. {{!}} History of Parliament Online |url=https://www.historyofparliamentonline.org/volume/1509-1558/member/gresham-sir-richard-1486-1549 |access-date=7 July 2022 |website=www.historyofparliamentonline.org |archive-date=7 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220707134006/https://www.historyofparliamentonline.org/volume/1509-1558/member/gresham-sir-richard-1486-1549 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 1597 the site was acquired by Sir [[Stephen Proctor]], who built [[Fountains Hall]]. Between 1627 and 1767 the estate was owned by the Messenger family. They sold it to [[William Aislabie (1700–1781)|William Aislabie]] who was responsible for combining it with the Studley Royal Estate.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.fountainsabbey.org.uk/downloads/FULL_TOME_160910_low.pdf?PHPSESSID=383bbdaed23a57a72977b75c006c2377 | title=Fountains Abbey and Studley Royal World heritage Site Management Plan 2009–14 | publisher=National Trust & English Heritage | year=2009 | access-date=7 February 2012 | page=5}} {{dead link|date=August 2024}}</ref>

==Current status==

The abbey is a Grade I [[listed building]] owned by the [[National Trust]] and is part of the designated ''[[Studley Royal Park]] including the Ruins of Fountains Abbey'' [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]].<ref name=":7">{{cite web |last=Centre |first=UNESCO World Heritage |title=Studley Royal Park including the Ruins of Fountains Abbey |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/372/ |access-date=7 July 2022 |website=UNESCO World Heritage Centre }}</ref>

[[Image:A lidar view of Fountains Abbey in Yorkshire.jpg|right|thumb|A [[lidar]] view of the abbey and landscape.]]

The archaeological excavation of the site began under the supervision of [[John Richard Walbran]], a Ripon antiquary who, in 1846, had published a paper ''On the Necessity of clearing out the Conventual Church of Fountains''.<ref name="DNB00">{{cite DNB|wstitle = Walbran, John Richard|first =Charles William|last =Sutton|author-link = Charles William Sutton|volume = 59|quote=''sources:''[Canon J. Raine's preface to ''Memorials of Fountains'', 1878, vol. ii; Memoir by ''Edward Peacock'', F.S.A., in Walbran's ''Guide to Ripon'', 11th edit. 1875; ''Ripon Millenary Record'', 1892, ii. 175; portraits are given in the last two works.]}}</ref> In 1966, the Abbey was placed in the guardianship of the Department of the Environment and the estate was purchased by the [[West Riding County Council]], who transferred ownership to [[North Yorkshire County Council]] in 1974. The National Trust bought the {{convert|674|acre|ha|adj=on}} Fountains Abbey and Studley Royal estate from North Yorkshire County Council in 1983.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.discoverbritainmag.com/fountains_abbey_and_studley_royal_the_wonder_of_the_north__1_3819923/|title=Fountains Abbey and Studley Royal: 'The Wonder of the North'|last=Hawksworth|first=Chris|date=24 October 2014|publisher=Discover Britain|access-date=7 June 2017}}</ref>

=== World Heritage Site designation ===
In 1986 the parkland in which the abbey is situated and the abbey was designated a [[World Heritage Site]] by [[UNESCO]]. It was recognised for fulfilling the criteria of "being a masterpiece of human creative genius", and "an outstanding example of a type of building or architectural or technological ensemble or landscape which illustrates significant stages in human history."<ref name=":7" />

=== National Trust ownership ===
Fountains Abbey is owned by the National Trust and maintained by [[English Heritage]]. The trust also owns [[Studley Royal Park]], and [[Fountains Hall]], and manages [[St Mary's, Studley Royal|St Mary's Church]], designed by [[William Burges]] and built around 1873 (owned by English Heritage).<ref>{{Cite web |title=St Mary's Church, Studley Royal |url=https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/st-marys-church-studley-royal/ |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=English Heritage}}</ref> All of these are significant features of the World Heritage Site.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/372/ |title=Studley Royal Park including the Ruins of Fountains Abbey – UNESCO World Heritage Centre  |access-date=7 February 2012}}</ref> In January 2010, Fountains Abbey and Studley Royal became two of the first National Trust properties to be included in [[Google Street View]], using the Google Trike.<ref>{{cite web |last=Kirkwood |first=Holly |date=21 January 2010 |title=National Trust castles now on Google Street View |url=http://www.countrylife.co.uk/property/article/439403/National-Trust-castles-now-on-Google-Street-View.html |access-date=30 January 2012 |work=Country Life}}</ref>

=== Exhibition and display ===
[[File:Fountains_Mill_-_geograph.org.uk_-_2065722.jpg|thumb|Fountains Mill]]
[[Fountains Mill]] is the former corn mill, built in the mid-twelfth century by the community.  There were two waterwheels installed, run from a [[leat]] taken from the Rover Skell.<ref>{{NHLE |desc=ABBEY MILL, Lindrick with Studley Royal and Fountains |num=1173325 |access-date=11 July 2022 }}</ref> It was later used as a sawmill, and in 1928 a turbine was installed to convert the building to the production of electricity.<ref>{{cite web |title=Fountains Abbey Watermill |url=https://www.spab.org.uk/mills/visit-a-mill/17456 |access-date=11 July 2022 |website=spab.org.uk |archive-date=11 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220711185704/https://www.spab.org.uk/mills/visit-a-mill/17456 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The turbine installation ended the building's over 800 years of continuous use as a mill.<ref>{{cite book |last=Goldsmith |first=Tessa |title=Fountains Abbey and Studley Royal, North Yorkshire : a souvenir guide |date=2011 |publisher=National Trust |others=Anna Groves, National Trust |isbn=978-1-84359-315-7 |location=[Great Britain] |pages=25 |oclc=772960735}}</ref>  It was refurbished and opened as an exhibition space in 2000.<ref>{{cite web |title=Fountains Abbey World Heritage Site {{!}} Historic Property Restoration |url=https://www.hprltd.co.uk/projects/fountains-abbey-world-heritage-site |access-date=11 July 2022 |website=www.hprltd.co.uk}}</ref> During 2022 the temporary exhibition was of work by the Yorkshire-based photographer [[Joe Cornish (photographer)|Joe Cornish]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Still Time to Wonder. An exhibition of photographs by Joe Cornish |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/fountains-abbey-and-studley-royal-water-garden/features/still-time-to-wonder-an-exhibition-by-joe-cornish- |access-date=11 July 2022 |website=National Trust }}</ref>

The Porter's Lodge, which was once the gatehouse to the abbey, houses a modern exhibition area with displays about the history of Fountains Abbey and how the monks lived. The centrepiece of the display is a scale model of the abbey at the time of the Dissolution. Following a suggestion by Commander Clare George Vyner,<ref>{{cite news | title = A Scale Model of Sountains Abbey as it was in 1539 | newspaper = The Sphere | location = London | date = 10 May 1952 }}</ref> it was designed by the architect and artist [[Arthur Edward Henderson]] (1870–1956), and constructed from plastic by P Kemp and E Wilson at workshops in [[Surbiton]].<ref>{{cite news | title = Fountains Abbey model | page = 2 | newspaper = Yorkshire Post and Leeds Intelligencer | location = Leeds | date = 9 April 1951}}</ref> The model, measuring some 10 feet by 7 feet and weighing about a ton, was donated on 23 April 1952.<ref>{{cite news | title = Model of Fountain's [''sic''] Abbey | page = 1 | newspaper = Yorkshire Post and Leeds Intelligencer | location = Leeds | date = 24 April 1952}}</ref> Henderson's book on Fountains Abbey compares photographs of various parts of the ruin with his drawings of how that section would have looked originally.<ref>{{cite book | last1 = Henderson | first1 = Arthur E. | title = Fountains Abbey Then and Now | location = London | publisher = [[Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge|SPCK]] |edition = 2nd | date = 1948}}</ref>

=== Climate crisis ===
Since 2006 assessment of the impact of climate change has been an essential requirement for the management of World Heritage Sites.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Phillips |first=Helen |date=1 November 2014 |title=Adaptation to Climate Change at UK World Heritage Sites: Progress and Challenges |url=https://doi.org/10.1179/1756750514Z.00000000062 |journal=The Historic Environment: Policy & Practice |volume=5 |issue=3 |pages=288–299 |doi=10.1179/1756750514Z.00000000062 |s2cid=128465870 |issn=1756-7505|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In early 2021 a National Trust press release stated that the abbey "is at risk of being irreparably damaged by flooding, with several instances in recent years [particularly in 2007] when the 12th-century ruins and water garden have been deluged by water".<ref>{{cite web |title=Historic river valley set for revival amid threat of climate change |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/press-release/historic-river-valley-set-for-revival-amid-threat-of-climate-change |access-date=7 July 2022 |website=National Trust }}</ref> Funding from the [[National Lottery Heritage Fund]] was subsequently awarded and was intended to help finance the Skell Valley Scheme, which would "rejuvenate 12 miles of the River Skell" to help minimize the risk of flooding.<ref>{{cite web |date=13 January 2021 |title=Historic river valley set for revival amid threat of climate change |url=https://nidderdaleaonb.org.uk/2021/01/13/historic-river-valley-set-for-revival-amid-threat-of-climate-change/ |publisher=Nidderdale AONB |accessdate=27 February 2021}}</ref>

'''Brimham Rocks''', once known as '''Brimham Crags''', is a 183.9-hectare (454-acre) biological [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]] (SSSI) and [[Geological Conservation Review]] (GCR) site, 8 miles (13 km) north-west of [[Harrogate]], North Yorkshire, England, on Brimham Moor in the [[Nidderdale AONB|Nidderdale]] [[Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty]]. The site, notified as SSSI in 1958, is an [[outcrop]] of [[Millstone Grit]], with small areas of [[Betula pendula|birch]] woodland and a large area of wet and dry [[heath]].

Brimham Rocks has SSSI status because of the value of its geology and the upland woodland and the acidic wet and dry heath habitats that support localised and specialised plant forms, such as [[Trientalis europaea|chickweed wintergreen]], [[Vaccinium vitis-idaea|cowberry]], [[Narthecium ossifragum|bog asphodel]] and three species of [[Ericaceae|heather]].<ref name="Citation BR SSSI" />

The site is known for its water- and weather-[[Erosion|eroded]] rocks, which were formed over 325 million years ago and have assumed fantastic shapes.<ref name="Croft 2009" /> In the 18th and 19th centuries, [[antiquarian]]s such as [[Hayman Rooke]] wondered whether they could have been at least partly carved by [[druid]]s,<ref name="Rooke 1786" /> an idea that ran concurrently with the popularity of [[James Macpherson]]'s ''[[Ossian|Fragments of Ancient Poetry]]'' of 1760, and a developing interest in [[Druidry (modern)|New-Druidism]]. For up to two hundred years, some stones have carried fanciful names, such as Druid's Idol, Druid's Altar and Druid's Writing Desk.

==Site location and SSSI designation==
[[File:Brimham Rocks from Flickr L 12.jpg|thumb|right|Heath, 2017]]
Brimham Rocks is a {{convert|183.9|ha|adj=on}} biological Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) and [[Geological Conservation Review]] (GCR) site,<ref name="Details, BR SSSI" >{{cite web |title=Designated sites view, Brimham Rocks SSSI, details |url=https://designatedsites.naturalengland.org.uk/SiteDetail.aspx?SiteCode=S1002279&SiteName=rock&countyCode=&responsiblePerson= |website=designatedsites.naturalengland.org.uk |publisher=Natural England |access-date=27 January 2020 |date=19 February 1988}}</ref> {{convert|8|mi}} south of [[Ripon]] on Brimham Moor in the [[Nidderdale AONB|Nidderdale]] [[Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty]] in [[North Yorkshire]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Photography Competition winners revealed |url=https://nidderdaleaonb.org.uk/2018/10/18/photography-competition-winners-revealed/ |website=Nidderdaleaonb.org.uk |publisher=Nidderdale AONB |access-date=15 February 2020 |date=18 October 2018 |archive-date=15 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200215172614/https://nidderdaleaonb.org.uk/2018/10/18/photography-competition-winners-revealed/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> It is {{convert|1.5|mi}} north of [[Summerbridge, North Yorkshire|Summerbridge]] and {{convert|3|mi}} east of [[Pateley Bridge]] and the [[River Nidd]].<ref name="MagicMap BR SSSI" >{{cite web |title=Magic Map Brimham Rocks SSSI |url=https://magic.defra.gov.uk/MagicMap.aspx?startTopic=Designations&activelayer=sssiIndex&query=HYPERLINK%3D%271002279%27 |website=magic.defra.gov.uk |publisher=Defra |access-date=27 January 2020}}</ref> The site is managed by the [[National Trust]] along with a visitor's centre, public facilities and a car park. Brimham Rocks is open throughout the year between around 8.30 am and dusk,<ref name="NT Brimham Rocks" >{{cite web |title=Brimham Rocks |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/brimham-rocks |website=nationaltrust.org.uk |publisher=National Trust |access-date=28 January 2020}}</ref><ref name="NT map of site" >{{cite web |title=Illustrated plan of Brimham Rocks |url=https://nt.global.ssl.fastly.net/documents/maps/1431729756358-brimham-rocks.pdf |website=nt.global.ssl.fastly.net |publisher=National Trust |access-date=28 January 2020 |archive-date=28 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200128151519/https://nt.global.ssl.fastly.net/documents/maps/1431729756358-brimham-rocks.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> but on 21 March 2020 closed due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom|coronavirus outbreak in the United Kingdom]].<ref name="NT Brimham Rocks website" >{{cite web |title=Brimham Rocks |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/brimham-rocks |website=nationaltrust.org.uk |publisher=National Trust |access-date=21 March 2020 |date=21 March 2020}}</ref> The site reopened fully in the summer of 2021, following the lifting of the UK Government measures to deal with COVID-19.<ref>{{cite web |title=Brimham Rocks opening times |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/brimham-rocks#Opening%20times |website=nationaltrust.org.uk |publisher=National Trust |access-date=28 July 2021}}</ref>

The site was [[SSSI notification|SSSI notified]] in 1958, with revisions in 1984 and on 19 February 1988. The site was listed for the value of its geology and because the "heath and bog habitats represent important examples of plant communities, formerly more widespread, which have been reduced by agricultural improvement, drainage and afforestation." Associated with the more well-known [[Outcrop|rocky outcrops]], are [[Betula pendula|birch]] woodland, [[Bog|acidic bogs]], wet and dry [[heath]], and plant communities which thrive when sheltered between the rocks and exposed on the [[Moorland|moor]].<ref name="Citation BR SSSI" />

==Geology==
[[File:Brimham Rocks 7 February 2020 (16).JPG|thumb|right|Turtle Rock, showing [[cross-bedding]]]]
Brimham Rocks are formed from a medium to coarse [[sandstone]] known both as the Lower Brimham Grit and also as the Lower Plompton Grit, one of a series of such sandstones laid down in the [[Pennsylvanian (geology)|later part of the Carboniferous period]] in what is now the [[Pennines|Pennine region]]. In formal terms this particular [[gritstone|grit]] which is between 10 and 30m thick, forms a part of the Hebden Formation, itself a sub-unit of the [[Millstone Grit]] Group. It was deposited 318-317 million years ago during the [[List of geochronologic names|Kinderscoutian]] substage of the [[Bashkirian]] stage.<ref>{{cite web |title=Lower Plompton Grit |url=https://www.bgs.ac.uk/lexicon/lexicon.cfm?pub=LPG |website=Lexicon of named rock units |publisher=British Geological Survey |access-date=12 April 2020}}</ref> The rock which has traditionally been referred to as [[Millstone Grit]], originated as [[fluvial processes|river-deposited]] sands in a [[river delta|delta environment]] and contains both [[feldspar]] and [[quartz]] pebbles.<ref>{{cite web |title=Lower Brimham Grit |url=https://www.bgs.ac.uk/lexicon/lexicon.cfm?pub=LOBM |website=Lexicon of named rock units |publisher=British Geological Survey |access-date=12 April 2020}}</ref> Deposition from moving water has resulted in the [[cross-bedding]] which is very evident in most of the outcrops.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Aitkenhead |first1=N. |title=The Pennines and adjacent areas |date=2002 |publisher=British Geological Survey |location=Nottingham |isbn=0852724241 |pages=52–55 |edition=Fourth}}</ref> Brimham Rocks has been described as "a classic geomorphological site, significant for studies of past and present weathering processes and their contribution to landscape evolution."
<ref name="Citation BR SSSI" >{{cite web |title=Brimham Rocks SSSI, citation |url=https://designatedsites.naturalengland.org.uk/PDFsForWeb/Citation/1002279.pdf |website=designatedsites.naturalengland.org.uk |publisher=Natural England |access-date=27 January 2020 |date=1988}}</ref>

Although discussion continues around the formation and date of [[tor (rock formation)|tors]] such as these throughout Britain, much of the development into the forms displayed at Brimham is likely to have taken place over the last 100,000 years before, during and after the last ice age – the [[Last Glacial Period|Devensian]]. Some disintegration of the rock strata may have occurred along weaknesses such as fault and fracture planes whilst still buried. Sub-aerial weathering has continued the process. The outcrops were exposed when [[glaciation|glacial action]], [[gelifluction]] and further weathering and water erosion removed the loose material which separated them.<ref name="Croft 2009" />

During periods of harsher climate, windblown-ice as well as particles of sand and dust have more effectively eroded weaker layers to give rise to these [[ventifact|wind-carved shapes]]. Such processes have created holes in some rocks, and left dust on the ground below.<ref>{{cite web |title=Step into Brimham |url=https://nt.global.ssl.fastly.net/brimham-rocks/documents/step-into-brimham.pdf |website=nt.global.ssl.fastly.net |publisher=National Trust |access-date=29 January 2020 |archive-date=29 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200129102045/https://nt.global.ssl.fastly.net/brimham-rocks/documents/step-into-brimham.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> Erosion continues, caused by weather and tourist numbers. One possibility for the mushroom shape of some stones is that they were exposed to sandblasting at ground level when an ice cap melted 18,000 years ago, narrowing the bases of outcrops, then they were subject to all-over sandblasting when the ice had gone, causing the irregular shapes.<ref name="Croft 2009" /> Due to this process the Idol rock, for example, will not exist for ever.<ref name="Croft 2009" />

===Druidic theories===
[[File:Brimham Rocks 7 February 2020 (7).JPG|thumb|right|Perforated rock, once thought to be an [[Oracle|oracular]] stone (now called Smartie Tube)]]
It was not until the early 20th century that it was understood that the rocks were created by natural forces.<ref name="Croft 2009" /> During the 18th and 19th centuries, some writers theorised that the rock-shaping could have been enhanced by [[Druid]]ic carving.<ref name="Paul Bennett 2011" >{{cite web |last1=Bennett |first1=Paul |title=Brimham Rocks, Hartwith, North Yorkshire |url=https://megalithix.wordpress.com/2011/03/21/brimham-rocks/ |website=megalithix.wordpress.com |publisher=The Northern Antiquarian |access-date=27 January 2020 |date=21 March 2011}}</ref> Their theories coincided with the growth of [[Druidry (modern)|Neo-Druidism]], and followed the 1760 publication of [[James Macpherson]]'s [[Ossian|''Fragments of Ancient Poetry'']].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Ossian |title=Fragments of Ancient Poetry, collected in the Highlands of Scotland |date=1760 |publisher=James Macpherson |location=Scotland |url=https://digital.nls.uk/early-gaelic-book-collections/archive/77455893 |access-date=5 February 2020}}</ref> After a lecture in 1786,<ref name="Rooke 1786" /> the opinion of the [[antiquary]] [[Hayman Rooke]] was reported in 1788 with mild scepticism by the ''Sheffield Register'':<ref name="Sheffield Register 13 Dec 1788" >{{cite news |last1=Rooke |first1=Hayman |title=Brimham Rocks in Yorkshire |url=https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/BL/0001113/17881213/020/0004?browse=true |access-date=1 February 2020 |work=Sheffield Register, Yorkshire, Derbyshire, & Nottinghamshire Universal Advertiser |agency=British Newspaper Archive |date=13 December 1788 |page=4 col.1}}</ref> {{blockquote|"The extraordinary position of these rocks is supposed to have been owing to some violent convulsion of nature, but it is evident, we are told, that art has not been wanting to render their situation yet more remarkable. Fragments of rocks obtained great regard, even veneration, from people of very remote antiquity: here they are found placed one on another, some having plainly the marks of the tool. This writer, though he does not venture to determine, conjectures that they are the work of the Druids. The [[Celtic Britons|Britons]] having had early communication with the [[Ancient Egypt|Egyptians]] and [[Phoenicia]]ns, it is probable, he thinks, that the Latter imparted their arts and religious ceremonies to the Druids, who would politically conceal them from the people, that by means of [[augury|auguries]] and [[divination]]s, the greater submission might be yielded to their decrees. To purposes of this kind Mr Rooke imagines these rocks to have been destined. They are various forms, some are [[Cult image|rock-idols]], others are [[Rocking stone|rocking-stones]], several have been perforated, in one instance, at least, quite through. To these our author assigns the name of the [[Oracle|oracular]] stone, supposing that hence the crafty Druids might contrive to deliver predictions and commands which the credulous people would receive as proceeding from the rock-deity. It is well known, that many, who enjoyed far superior advantages for religious knowledge, have in later times employed such deceitful and scandalous methods to promote their ambitious and tyrannical views. (Whether it was thus in the very remote and uncultured periods to which Mr Rooke alludes, must remain in the uncertainty wherein time has involved this with many other points of historical [[wikt:disquisition|disquisition]])."<ref name="Sheffield Register 13 Dec 1788" />}}

In 1844, Druidic theories were strong enough for the ''Worcester Journal'' to publish a list of "British monuments, commonly called Druidical," to correct misunderstandings, including those by "antiquarian writers of celebrity." The list included the Rock Idol at Brimham Rocks.<ref name="Worcester 25 Apr 1844" >{{cite news |title=On Druidical remains |url=https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000150/18440425/029/0004 |access-date=2 February 2020 |work=Worcester Journal |agency=British Newspaper Archive |date=25 April 1844 |page=4 col.1}}</ref> [[Samuel Lewis (publisher)|Lewis's 1848 ''Topographical Dictionary'']] describes the area: "... at Brimham are masses of vast rocks spread in the wildest profusion over a tract of nearly 40 acres, the ancient resort of the Druids".<ref>{{cite web |title=Hartlip - Harwich A Topographical Dictionary of England. |url=https://www.british-history.ac.uk/topographical-dict/england/pp427-431#h3-s17 |website=British History Online |publisher=S Lewis, London 1848 |access-date=6 January 2025}}</ref> By 1849 [[John Richard Walbran]], writing about erosion as the cause of the rocks' shapes, hesitated to support Druidical theories.<ref name="Walbran 1849" >{{cite book |last1=Walbran |first1=John Richard |title=The pictorial pocket guide to Ripon and Harrogate : with topographical observations on Studley-Royal, Brimham Rocks, Hackfall, and the monastic remains of Fountains and Bolton (via Haithi Trust) |date=1849 |publisher=W. Harrison |location=Ripon |page=84 |edition=3rd |chapter-url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.hnzn43&view=1up&seq=101 |access-date=11 February 2020 |chapter=Brimham Rocks}}</ref>

Nevertheless, in 1849, Druidic theories were still influential. [[John Williams (Ab Ithel)]], described Brimham Rocks in a poetic manner as if they were partly created by the hand of man: "Brimham Rocks, where amidst great natural acclivities, and on the verge of [[precipice]]s, ancient architects of the school of the builders of the [[Richard Monckton Milnes, 1st Baron Houghton|Tomb of Laius]],<ref>{{cite web |last1=Monckton Milnes, Lord Houghton (1809–1885) |first1=Richard |title=The Tomb of Laius |url=https://www.bartleby.com/270/9/60.html |website=bartleby.com |access-date=10 February 2020}}</ref> seem to have derived an intense pleasure in vanquishing and triumphing over the difficulties which nature opposed to their exertions."<ref>{{cite news |title=Cromlech |url=https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000914/18491117/035/0004 |access-date=2 February 2020 |work=Cardiff and Merthyr Guardian, Glamorgan, Monmouth, and Brecon Gazette |agency=British Newspaper Archive |date=17 November 1849 |page=4 col.2}}</ref>

By 1890 Druidic theories were dying out, leaving some rock names to bear witness to past ideas. The ''Pateley Bridge & Nidderdale Herald'' quoted from Professor Phillips' ''Geology of Yorkshire'': {{blockquote|"The wasting power of the atmosphere is very consipicuous in these rocks; searching out their secret lamination; working perpendicular furrows and horizontal cavities; wearing away the bases, and thus bringing slow but sure destruction on the whole of the exposed masses. Those that remain of the rocks of Brimham are but perishing memorials of what have been destroyed."<ref>{{cite news |title=Brimham Rocks|url=https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0001273/18900913/121/0007 |access-date=13 February 2020 |work=Pateley Bridge & Nidderdale Herald |agency=British Newspaper Archive |date=13 September 1890 |page=7 col 6}}</ref>}}

===Rock names===
[[File:Great Cannon Rock 22 February 2020 (3).JPG|thumb|right|''Great Cannon'' is one of the earliest rock names on this site]]
Many of the rock names have been used for over a hundred years. Some fanciful names may have been invented by the Rocks House caretakers in their efforts to amuse visitors. Some appear to have been inspired by antiquarians who adhered to Druidical theories about their origins. Just a few names, such as the Noonstone whose shadow indicated midday,{{refn|The Noonstone is marked on the OS map and Defra Magicmap, to the west of the SSSI site, next to Throstle Nest and Adams Ale spring.|group=nb}} and old local names, Great Cannon and Little Cannon (now the Smartie Tube), may come from an earlier tradition. In his 1786 lecture, ''Some account of the Brimham rocks in Yorkshire'', Hayman Rooke mentions the Idol Rock, the Great Cannon, and the Noonstone next to which a fire was lit on Midsummer Eve.<ref name="Rooke 1786" >{{cite book |last1=Rooke |first1=Hayman |title=Lecture: Some account of the Brimham rocks in Yorkshire (Reproduction from British Library) |date=2018|orig-date=25 May 1786 |publisher=Eighteenth Century Collections Online (ECCO) |location=Society of Antiquaries |ref=ESTCID: T160150|isbn=9781379617075 }}</ref>

In 1844 the ''Worcester Journal'' mentions the Rock Idol,<ref name="Worcester 25 Apr 1844" /> and in 1843 the ''Leeds Times'' mentions the Rocking Stones, Lovers' Leap, Baboon's Head, Pulpit Rock, Parson's Head, Yoke of Oxen, Frog and Tortoise, Serpent's Head, Dancing Bear, Druid's Writing Desk, Druid's Aerial Altar, Druid's Coffin, Sphinx, Oyster Shell, Mushroom, Idol Rock, and Cannon Rocks.<ref name="Leeds Times 21 Oct 1843" /> In 1849 J.R. Walbran mentions the Rocking Stones and illustrates the Anvil and Porpoise Head.<ref name="Walbran 1849" /> In 1906 the writer Harry Speight mentions the Elephant Rock, the Porpoise Head, the Dancing Bear, the Boat Rock, the Idol and the Rocking Stones. The identity of the Porpoise Head rock has been forgotten, although it appears in a drawing by Walbran.<ref name="Harry Speight 1906" />

The mention of Druids appears in ''Brimham Rocks, the wonder of Nidderdale'' ({{circa|1920}}) by journalist Herbert W. Ogle (1871–1940) of [[Otley]]. He lists Druid's Head, Druid's Writing desk, Druid's Castle, Druid's Pulpit, Druid's Parlour, Druid's Kitchen, Druid's Coffin, Druid's telescope "and so on." The Parlour and Kitchen no longer exist.<ref name="Ogle ca 1920" >{{cite book |last1=Ogle |first1=Herbert W. |title=Brimham Rocks, the wonder of Nidderdale |date=1920 |publisher=Fred Burn |location=Brimham Rocks}}</ref> At the far end of the Eye of the Needle were once the Druid's Caves, which included a Parlour and Bedroom, but they have been exposed or obliterated by a rock fall. Other rock names mentioned in 1920 are Oyster Shell, Rocking Stones, Baboon Rock, Mushroom Rock, Wishing Rock, Yoke of Oxen, Boat Rock (also known as the Druid's Altar), Boat Rocking Stone ("first discovered to be movable in 1786"), Dancing Bear, Rhinoceros Head, Anvil Rock, Pivot Rock, Lovers' Leap, Frog and Tortoise, Cannon Rocks, Split Rock, Sphinx Rock, Rabbit Rock, Elephant's Head, Dog Rock (possibly the Watchdog) and Tiger's Head.<ref name="Ogle ca 1920"/>

In his ''Guide to Brimham Rocks'' published in 1863, local historian [[William Grainge]] wrote "These names are frequently changed by the innovating, garrulous guide, who has changed the ''Baboon's Head'' to the ''Gorilla's'', and the ''Yoke of Oxen'' to the ''Bulls of Babylon'', which unsettling of nomenclature he calls keeping pace with the times. Unique as the rocks are amongst the freaks of nature, there is nearly as much originality about the ''guide'' but infinitely less grandeur."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Grainge |first1=William |title=The Tourist's Guide to Brimham Rocks, Hartwith, Yorkshire, Second Edition. (Extracted from a Larger Work by the Same Author, Entitled, Nidderdale, Etc.) |date=1865 |publisher=Thomas Thorpe |location=London |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sR5bAAAAcAAJ |access-date=18 April 2021}}</ref>

<gallery class="center">

Brimham Rocks by Walbran 1856 (a).jpg|Anvil and Porpoise Head, 1856

In 2020 the [[National Trust]] produced ''Spot the Rocks'', a discovery trail sheet for children, listing eleven of the rock names. ==Biological site content==
Peat was once dug on Brimham Moor.<ref name="Ogle ca 1920" /> Heather-burning, grazing, management for [[Hunting and shooting in the United Kingdom|shooting]], and air pollution from [[Industrial Revolution|industrialisation]] plus two hundred years of footfall from visitors, has limited [[biodiversity]] especially around the rocky outcrop. Some of the heath has not been affected.<ref name="Croft 2009" />

===Flora===
At the east side of the Brimham Rocks site [[Vaccinium vitis-idaea|cowberry]] grows, it is "a northern species found mostly in Yorkshire."<ref name="Croft 2009" /> On the dry heathland by the rocks, on shallow soil with sand,<ref name="Croft 2009" /> grows a scattering of [[Quercus robur|oak]], [[Sorbus aucuparia|rowan]] and [[Betula pendula|silver birch]], although its main cover is [[Deschampsia flexuosa|wavy hair-grass]], [[Vaccinium myrtillus|bilberry]], [[Erica cinerea|bell heather]] and [[Calluna vulgaris|ling]], with [[Pteridium aquilinum|bracken]] under the rock stacks. Birch grows on the north-east side in a regenerating forest.<ref name="Citation BR SSSI" /><ref name="NT moorland conservation" /> Until at least 1920, [[Empetrum nigrum|crowberry]] used to grow here.<ref name="Ogle ca 1920" /> In the north woodland is [[Trientalis europaea|chickweed wintergreen]], which is "uncommon" and "of note."<ref name="Citation BR SSSI" />

==Maintenance==
The [[National Trust]] has a Countryside and Community Manager at Brimham Rocks to oversee maintenance.<ref>{{cite web |title=Protecting the natural habitat at Brimham Rocks |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/brimham-rocks/profiles/protecting-the-natural-habitat-at-brimham-rocks |website=nationaltrust.org.uk |publisher=National Trust |access-date=28 January 2020}}</ref> On all [[habitat]]s on this site, [[fertiliser]] and [[pesticide]]s would harm the flora and fauna, and should not be used. The use of [[herbicide]] is discouraged, it should be used with "extreme care."<ref name="Management BR SSSI" /> A [[Herbicide#Selectivity (all plants or specific plants)|selective herbicide]] is used on [[Pteridium aquilinum|bracken]], however.<ref name="NT moorland conservation" >{{cite web |title=Moorland conservation at Brimham Rocks |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/brimham-rocks/features/our-conservation-projects-on-heather-moorland |website=nationaltrust.org.uk |publisher=National Trust |access-date=28 January 2020}}</ref>

A high proportion of the Brimham Rocks site is recognised [[common land]], where local farmers may graze their livestock. National Trust wardens work the year round to maintain this site. The work includes maintaining visitor paths and roads, bird-recording, controlling bracken and silver birch, and removing litter and storm-damaged trees.<ref name="Croft 2009" />

===Rocks===
Where appropriate, the rocks should be kept clear of vegetation and rock debris, so that the geology remains visible. Building developments and trees should not conceal the exposed rocks. "Widespread [[rock climbing]] activities and high visitor numbers ... need to be balanced with the protection of the rock features." Collecting of [[Type specimen (mineralogy)|geological specimens]] is not allowed.<ref name="Management BR SSSI" >{{cite web |title=Brimham Rocks SSSI, management |url=https://designatedsites.naturalengland.org.uk/PDFsForWeb/VAM/1002279.pdf |website=designatedsites.naturalengland.gov.uk |publisher=Natural England |access-date=27 January 2020 |date=5 May 2005}}</ref>

===Heath===
The plants on both wet and dry upland heath have developed a requirement for acidic and nutrient-poor soil, which is at least partially affected by underlying layers of [[Sphagnum]] moss, or [[peat]]. Thus the prevalent mixture of low shrubs, [[Ericaceae|heather]] and [[Eriophorum|cottongrass]] will support a large number of animals and insects. Careful maintenance of dry [[heath]] requires just enough livestock [[grazing]] to keep down trees and shrubs, but minimum winter grazing to protect those same shrubs. [[Animal feed]] should not be placed on this habitat because its detritus and animal dung would enrich the soil. Where necessary, grazing should be temporarily withheld, to allow the vegetation to recover.<ref name="Management BR SSSI" /> Although as of 2020 local farmers have not used their grazing rights recently, the National Trust may reintroduce this heath maintenance method.<ref name="Croft 2009" />

Most wet heaths require little management, but if necessary a little light grazing may be used to prevent encroachment of trees and shrubs. Heavy grazing should be avoided on wet heath because it damages the peaty soil. [[Controlled burn|Heather-burning]] should only take place with the agreement of [[English Nature]], because burning can destroy adjacent woods, destroy some plants, destroy cover for certain nesting birds, encourage [[erosion]], and encourage dominance of [[bracken]] and [[Ulex|gorse]]. Cutting, if done without machinery, is a good alternative to burning, because it preserves the soil. Artificial [[drainage]] of wet heath is discouraged, because it would change the nature of the habitat.<ref name="Management BR SSSI" />

===Woodland===
This is [[Upland and lowland|upland]], semi-natural woodland. The clean air and high rainfall have made it a habitat for [[flora]] and [[fauna]] which is less commonly found in lowland [[woodland]]. However, beneficial previous and present management of this woodland has protected it from overgrazing, allowing plants and animals to proliferate. Where appropriate, woodland may be protected from livestock by fencing, it may be partially [[Coppicing|coppiced]] to let in light, or trees may be allowed to grow and die naturally. [[Invasive species|Invasive]], not-native plants such as [[rhododendron]] should be removed. Wet woodland should be left alone where possible, allowing trees to grow and fall naturally. Any underplanted [[Pinophyta|conifer]]s should be removed. The mix of plants where the woodland and heath blend should be retained.<ref name="Management BR SSSI" />

==Development and risk assessment==
For assessment, Natural England has divided the site into five units. Numbers one ({{convert|73.0503|ha|km2 sqmi|sigfig=4}}), two ({{convert|84.6384|ha|km2 sqmi|sigfig=4}}) and four ({{convert|0.8937|ha|km2 sqmi|sigfig=4}}) are described as upland dwarf [[shrub]] [[heath]], and units three ({{convert|2.7438|ha|km2 sqmi|sigfig=4}}) and five ({{convert|2.5707|ha|km2 sqmi|sigfig=4}}) are upland [[Deciduous|broadleaved]] mixed and [[taxus baccata|yew]] [[woodland]].<ref name="MagicMap 5 units" >{{cite web |title=MagicMap Brimham Rocks SSSI site units |url=https://magic.defra.gov.uk/MagicMap.aspx?startTopic=Designations&activelayer=siteunitIndex&query=HYPERLINK%3D%271016279%27 |website=magic.defra.gov.uk |publisher=Defra |access-date=4 February 2020 |date=2020}}</ref>

The units were assessed in 2012 and 2013, when all units were adjudged unfavourable and recovering, except unit 4 which was favourable. Plans for [[Habitat conservation|management]] of units 1 and 2 were in place, and recovery was expected. That left woodland units 3 and 5 still with problems. Woodland from unit 3 was encroaching onto unit 1 (supposed to be heath). Unit 3 had not enough ground [[flora]], although it did have naturally [[Regeneration (biology)|regenerating]] trees. The problem with woodland unit 5 is that there was almost no [[Understory|understorey]], and not enough ground cover plants, although it did have some new [[Tree#Overview|sapling]]s. Both wood units 3 and 5 had some encroaching [[Pteridium aquilinum|bracken]]. Unit 4, the [[Tourist attraction|visitor attraction]] with the rocks, was considered favourable because visitor damage did not appear noticeable, and there were not too many plants concealing the [[Stratum|geology]]. The trees which conceal views from the rocks were not mentioned.<ref name="Condition BR SSSI" >{{cite web |title=Brimham Rocks SSSI, condition |url=https://designatedsites.naturalengland.org.uk/ReportUnitCondition.aspx?SiteCode=S1002279&ReportTitle=Brimham%20Rocks%20SSSI |website=designatedsites.naturalengland.gov.uk |publisher=Natural England |access-date=27 January 2020 |date=2013}}</ref><ref name="Units BR SSSI" >{{cite web |title=Brimham Rocks SSSI, units |url=https://designatedsites.naturalengland.org.uk/SiteUnitList.aspx?SiteCode=S1002279&SiteName=rock&countyCode=&responsiblePerson=&unitId=&SeaArea=&IFCAArea= |website=designatedsites.naturalengland.gov.uk |publisher=Natural England |access-date=27 January 2020}}</ref> Nevertheless, the rocky part of the site receives more than 175,000 people including families, climbers, naturalists and others every year, and this does affect the biodiversity of the rocky section.<ref name="Croft 2009" />

On 17 February 2018 at Brimham Rocks the Police, the [[North Yorkshire]] [[National parks of England and Wales|National Parks]] and the [[Royal Society for the Protection of Birds|RSPB]] launched Operation Owl, "an initiative to tackle the illegal persecution of [[Bird of prey|birds of prey]] in the county. This was because North Yorkshire had the highest raptor persecution record in the country, and they wanted to do "random swoops" in places where they believed this might be happening. They were also asking the public to report "illegal [[Bird trapping|pole traps]], [[poisoning|poisoned bait]] and [[habitat]] disturbance, associated with "shooting interests."<ref>{{cite web |title=Police join forces with other agencies to tackle persecution of birds of prey: Operation Owl |url=https://www.harrogate-news.co.uk/2018/02/17/police-join-forces-agencies-tackle-persecution-birds-prey/ |website=harrogate.news.co.uk |publisher=Harrogate Informer |access-date=28 January 2020 |date=17 February 2018}}</ref> Pole traps are "spring-loaded traps fixed to the top of posts which have been [[Crime|outlawed]] since [[Victorian era|Victorian times]]." The traps themselves are legal for catching vermin (e.g. rats) if used low on the ground and in tunnels, but are illegal on poles where birds will be killed.<ref>{{cite web |title=North Yorkshire Police call on public to prevent slaughter of birds of prey |url=https://www.harrogateadvertiser.co.uk/news/north-yorkshire-police-call-public-prevent-slaughter-birds-prey-708512 |website=harrogateadvertiser.co.uk |publisher=Harrogate Advertiser |access-date=28 January 2020 |date=17 February 2018}}</ref>

In September 2018 a group of climbers assisted the National Trust in "to return many of the locations between Cubic Block and Titfield Thunderbolt at Brimham to their previous airy and open state," that is, they removed large trees and other growth which had caused obstructions to the climbing experience at Brimham Rocks.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Clarke |first1=Paul |title=Climbers and National Trust work together to re-vitalise Brimham Rocks |url=https://www.thebmc.co.uk/brimham-rocks-cleanup |website=thebmc.co.uk |publisher=British Mountaineering Council |access-date=28 January 2020 |date=1 October 2018}}</ref>

At 8.45 pm on 1 June 2018, in "an act of mindless destruction," five youths were observed destroying one of Brimham Rocks' balancing stones by pushing it from its high spot so that it broke on the ground. The balancing stone had taken 320 million years to form by [[erosion]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hartley-Parkinson |first1=Richard |title=Bunch of idiots destroy 32,000,000 years of history in a few stupid seconds |url=https://metro.co.uk/2018/06/13/bunch-idiots-destroy-320000000-years-history-stupid-seconds-7628443/ |website=metro.co.uk |publisher=Metro |access-date=31 January 2020 |date=13 June 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Police investigate 'dangerous' act of vandalism at Brimham Rocks|url=https://www.harrogateadvertiser.co.uk/news/crime/police-investigate-dangerous-act-of-vandalism-at-brimham-rocks-1-9194809|work=Harrogate Advertiser|date=6 June 2018|access-date=7 June 2018}}</ref>

==Site history==
Hayman Rooke found [[Tumulus|barrows]] and stone circles in this area before 1786:<ref name="Rooke 1786" /> {{blockquote|"About eighty yards S.W. of the ... Great Cannon is a large [[tumulus]] of earth and stones one hundred and fifty feet in circumference: on the west side there seems to have been a little ditch and [[vallum]],{{refn|Rooke concluded that the ditch and vallum had been robbed out|group=nb}} which probably inclosed the tumulus ... About a quarter of a mile farther to the west is a [[Stone circles in the British Isles and Brittany|Druid circle]],{{refn|The 1854 OS map shows the Druids' Circle about 80 yards north-west of Rocks House (now the Visitor Centre/Brimham House), and about 50 yards west of the trig point.|group=nb}} with a vallum of earth and stones, thirty feet diameter. It is exactly of the same construction as those on Stanton Moor,{{refn|See the stone circles [[Nine Ladies]] on [[Stanton Moor]], Derbyshire, and [[Doll Tor]] west of Stanton Moor|group=nb}} in the [[Peak District|peak of Derbyshire]]. There are likewise several small tumuli. Thirteen of them are arranged in a kind of circle, the largest not above eighteen feet diameter. They are formed of earth and large stones. Two of these I opened: towards the bottom the effects of fire appeared on the stones, and ashes were scattered about, but there were no [[urns]] to be fournd."<ref name="Rooke 1786" />}}

Katie Croft, in the National Trust guidebook, ''Brimham Rocks'' (2009), says that these barrows have not been found. The name, ''Birnebeam,''<ref name="Croft 2009" >{{cite book |last1=Croft |first1=Katie |title=Brimham Rocks |date=2009 |publisher=Park Lane Press for National Trust |location=Swindon, Wiltshire |isbn=9781911384908}}</ref> or  ''Birnebaha'',<ref name="NT Brimham Rocks House" /> meaning "tree in clearing," refers to Brimham in the [[Domesday Book]] of 1086. [[Fountains Abbey]] owned it as [[pasture]] by 1252, and had a [[Fish pond|fishpool]],<ref name="Croft 2009" /> then at the [[Reformation]] it reverted to [[The Crown]] from the 1530s.<ref name="NT Brimham Rocks House" /> It was granted to [[Richard Gresham]], then in 1780 Lord Grantley bought it.<ref name="NT Brimham Rocks House" /> Brimham Moor was fox-hunting country by the 18th century, used by Colonel Thornton's Hunt.<ref>{{cite news |title=Swinnow House to be Lett |url=https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000236/17940113/010/0002 |access-date=24 February 2020 |work=Leeds Intelligencer |agency=British Newspaper Archive |date=13 January 1794 |page=2 col.3}}</ref> Later, around 1827, the [[Henry Lascelles, 2nd Earl of Harewood|Earl of Harewood]]'s [[foxhound]]s would meet at the crossroads on Brimham Moor, making it possible to hunt across the Rocks since there could be no standing crops there.<ref>{{cite news |title=The Earl of Harewood's foxhounds |url=https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000266/18271208/011/0003 |access-date=2 February 2020 |work=Yorkshire Gazette |agency=British Newspaper Archive |date=8 December 1827 |page=3 col.6}}</ref>

In April 1842 several newspapers voiced disappointment that "the appearance of that beautiful spot called Brimham Rocks ... has been greatly injured by the burning off of all the [[moss]] &c. with which they were formerly covered." The identity of the offenders was unknown.<ref>{{cite news |title=Brimham Rocks |url=https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000193/18420423/136/0005 |access-date=1 February 2020 |work=Leeds Intelligencer |agency=British Newspaper Archive |date=23 April 1842 |page=5 col.4}}</ref> In early May of the same year, vandals set the moorland around Brimham Rocks on fire several times, taking advantage of a severe drought.<ref>{{cite news |title=The weather |url=https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000266/18420514/020/0005 |access-date=2 February 2020 |work=Yorkshire Gazette |agency=British Newspaper Archive |date=14 May 1842 |page=5 col.2}}</ref>

A newspaper report of 1846 gives a glimpse of local life and an odd reference to Brimham Rocks. At an August [[Ripon Racecourse|Ripon Race]] meeting, a nameless five-year-old brown [[mare]], who was both a [[Field hunter|hunter]] and also a daughter of Sheet Anchor, was disqualified after some drama.<ref name="Yorks Gazette 22 Aug 1846" /> {{blockquote|"The Sheet Anchor mare, whose Jockey was attired in very primitive [[Jockey#Racing colours|colours]], and flourished a stout [[Fraxinus|ash]] sapling, took the lead at a furious pace, came tearing past the [[Grandstand|Grand Stand]], amidst loud cries of, ''Hurrah for [[Pateley Bridge|Pateley Brig]]'' and kept it once round, when the instant he was headed,{{refn|When a racehorse is headed, it means that he is at least briefly in front of other horses|group=nb}} his [[Singlestick|cudgel]] was brought into vigorous play, but all to no purpose, though he belaboured her in true Brimham Rocks style to the very confines of the distance, which he failed to reach in time."<ref name="Yorks Gazette 22 Aug 1846" >{{cite news |title=Ripon meeting, Yorkshire |url=https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000266/18460822/058/0008 |access-date=2 February 2020 |work=Yorkshire Gazette |agency=British Newspaper Archive |date=22 August 1846 |page=8 col.3}}</ref>}}

===Crime===
In August 2014 the body of Gemma Simpson was found at Brimham Rocks. That December Martin Bell, who had [[schizophrenia]], pleaded guilty to [[Manslaughter in English law|manslaughter]], and was sentenced to a minimum of twelve years' imprisonment. In May 2000 he had smoked [[cannabis]] with her, "bludgeoned and stabbed" her to death, left her in a bath for some days, dismembered her, then buried her body at a secret location at Brimham Rocks for fourteen years. In July 2014 he confessed to the murder and disclosed the location of the body, at [[Scarborough, North Yorkshire|Scarborough]] police station.<ref>{{cite web |title=Gemma Simpson death: Martin Bell jailed for 12 years |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-leeds-30548799 |website=bbc.co.uk |publisher=British Broadcasting Company |access-date=22 March 2020 |date=19 December 2014}}</ref>
