[[Historic house museum|Historic House Museum]] | accreditation = | key_holdings = | collections = | collection_size = | visitors = 24,500 (2015/6) | founder = | director = David Morgan | president = | ceo = | chairperson = | curator = | architect = {{plainlist| *[[Walter Brierley]] *George Dillistone (Garden)}} | historian = | owner = [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] | public_transit = Buses from [[York railway station|York Station]]{{rail-interchange|gb|rail}} to [[Dringhouses]]{{cite web|url=https://www.itravelyork.info/downloads/file/2/york-bus-route-map |title= York Bus Route Map |access-date=20 August 2023}} | parking = {{plainlist| *See website *On site: Accessible Parking}} | network = | website = {{URL|www.nationaltrust.org.uk/goddards-house-and-garden}} | embedded = {{infobox designation list | embed = yes | designation1 = Grade I | designation1_offname = Goddards and Attached Gateway, Terrace and Loggia to Side and Rear | designation1_date = 24 June 1983 | designation1_number = {{National Heritage List for England |num=1256461|short=yes}} | designation1_free1name = Client | designation1_free1value = Noel Goddard Terry | designation1_free2name = Completed | designation1_free2value = 1927 | designation2 = Grade II* | designation2_offname = Number 25 Including Carriage Entrance | designation2_date = 24 June 1983 | designation2_number = {{National Heritage List for England |num=1256505|short=yes}} }} }} '''Goddards House and Garden''' is an [[Arts and Crafts movement|Arts and Crafts]] house in [[Dringhouses]], [[York]], England. It was built in 1927 for Noel and Kathleen Terry of the famed chocolate-manufacturing family [[Terry's]] with the house designed by local architect [[Walter Brierley]] and the garden by George Dillistone. The [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] acquired the property in 1984 to use as regional offices and the garden is open to visitors seasonally. The house is a Grade I [[listed building]] and the carriage entrance to the property is Grade II* listed. ==Design== ===House=== [[File:Goddards york herbaceous border.jpg|thumb|left|View of the house and herbaceous border|alt=a grass lawn and a border of flowering plants in front of a large redbrick house.]] Goddards was the last major project of Walter Brierley who died in 1926 whilst the house was still under construction. His own home (the Grade II* listed [[Bishopsbarns]]){{NHLE|num=1256793|desc=Bishopsbarns|accessdate=25 April 2019}} in St George's Place, York, was in the same street that Noel and Kathleen Terry lived in and {{convert|1|km|mi|1|order=flip}} from Goddards.{{cite web|url=http://dlhg.weebly.com/uploads/3/9/0/5/3905109/the_terry_trail_dlhg.pdf |title=The Terry Trail |website=dlhg.weebly.com|access-date=23 June 2016}} One of the notable architectural features of the house is the [[Vault (architecture)|vaulted ceiling]] in the drawing room which is similar to Brierley's own home with the [[plasterwork]] in both houses attributed to George Bankart, probably George P Bankart in both cases, rather than his son George E Bankart, with whom he wrote books about the craft.{{cite web|url=http://sculpture.gla.ac.uk/view/person.php?id=msib2_1206485096|title=George Percy Bankart|website=Mapping the Practice and Profession of Sculpture in Britain and Ireland 1851–1951, University of Glasgow History of Art and HATII, online database 2011|access-date=29 June 2016|archive-date=18 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160918225756/http://sculpture.gla.ac.uk/view/person.php?id=msib2_1206485096|url-status=dead}} The [[National Heritage List for England]] describes Goddards as “the finest surviving example of the work of Walter Brierley, the Lutyens of the north”,{{NHLE|num=1256461 |desc=Goddards House and Garden|accessdate=23 June 2016|fewer-links=yes}} and it still retains many of the original fixtures including its Arts and Crafts wallpapers and panelling and the staircase with its oak carving. The exterior of the house features handmade locally produced bricks arranged in geometric patterns and decorative chimney stacks typical of a Brierley building.{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/goddards-house-and-garden/documents/download-the-goddards-the-art-of-design-leaflet.pdf |title=The Art of Design |website=www.nationaltrust.org.uk| access-date=29 June 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160828094725/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/goddards-house-and-garden/documents/download-the-goddards-the-art-of-design-leaflet.pdf |archive-date=28 August 2016}} Goddards was built by William Anelay whose initial estimate for the project, including the carriage entrance, was £25,980 ({{Inflation|UK|25980|1926|r=-4|fmt=eq|cursign=£}}),{{Inflation-fn|UK}} however the work suffered a number of delays and was not finished until after the family had moved into the house.{{cite web|url=http://www.yorkpress.co.uk/features/features/15490349.GODDARDS_THROUGH_THE_AGES__Noel_Terry_s_former_home_hits_90/ |title=GODDARDS THROUGH THE AGES: Noel Terry's former home hits 90 |work=York Press |date=24 August 2017 |access-date=14 November 2017}} Copies of the original plans are displayed in the house.{{cite web|url=https://villacastagnadaylesford.com.au/2017/10/23/goddards-in-york-an-arts-and-crafts-house-made-with-chocolate/|title=Goddard's in York: An Arts and Crafts House Made with Chocolate|publisher=Villa Castagna |date=23 October 2017|access-date=29 August 2018}} {{clear|left}} ===Garden=== [[File:Goddards York lily pool and lawn.jpg|thumb|left|The lawn beside the lily pool was originally a rose garden, the layout of which is revealed by [[cropmark]]s.|alt=a stone-edged cruciform pond on the left, on the right is a lawn with patterns formed by parched grass.]] In 1925 George Dillistone, a landscape architect from [[Tunbridge Wells]] who worked with [[Edwin Lutyens|Lutyens]] at [[Castle Drogo]], was hired to design the garden at Goddards. The design evolved over a number of years and plans were still being developed as late as 1935,{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/documents/abc-bulletin-summer-2013.pdf|title=Arts Buildings Collections Bulletin: Summer Issue August 2013|publisher=National Trust|pages=9–10|access-date=28 December 2017}} by which time Dillistone had become vice-president of the [[Landscape Institute|Institute of Landscape Architects]].{{cite book|title=Reflections on Landscape: The Lives and Work of Six British Landscape Architects|editor=Sheila Harvey|publisher=Gower Technical Press|year=1987|isbn=9780291397089|page=107|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lXdRAAAAMAAJ&dq=%22Institute+of+Landscape+Architects%22+dillistone&q=dillistone|access-date=25 September 2018}} In keeping with the style of the house, the four acre garden at Goddards was divided into several distinct areas, including a terrace and a series of rooms separated by shrubs, hedges and a [[herbaceous border]];{{cite web |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/goddards-house-and-garden/features/the-gardens-at-goddards- | title= National Trust Goddards House and Garden: The Gardens| access-date= 27 June 2016}} all of these elements illustrate the Arts and Crafts nature of the garden.{{cite book|last=Rutherford |first=Sarah |date=2013 |title=The Arts and Crafts Garden (shire library) |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rQ3DCwAAQBAJ |publisher=Bloomsbury |pages=19–21 |isbn=9780747813453}} The enclosures included a [[tennis]] court (restored in 2016) and a [[bowling green]] used as a [[croquet]] lawn.{{cite web|url=http://www.yorkshirepost.co.uk/news/anyone-for-tennis-at-home-of-chocolate-dynasty-1-7971987 |title=Anyone for tennis at home of chocolate dynasty? |work=[[The Yorkshire Post]] |date=19 June 2016 |access-date=26 June 2016}} The centrepiece of the garden is a cruciform lily pool which is fed from a semi-circular [[reflecting pool]] and was originally surrounded by a rose garden.{{cite journal|title=One Vision|journal=[[The Garden (Royal Horticultural Society)|The Garden]]|volume=121|year=1996|pages=328–331|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=x80jAQAAMAAJ|access-date=25 September 2018}} Beyond this area the garden slopes downwards to [[York Racecourse]], ([[Knavesmire]]) across which it was possible to walk to where, in 1926, Terry's had built their [[The Chocolate Works|factory]], with its distinctive [[clock tower]] visible from the garden.{{cite web|url=http://www.c20society.org.uk/botm/terrys-clock-tower-york/ |title=Building of the Month: Terry's Clock Tower, York |website=www.c20society.org.uk |date=April 2016 |access-date=25 June 2016}} Typical of this style of garden the landscaping becomes less formal further from the house with paths leading down through a [[rock garden]] at the far end of the garden. The wildlife in the garden included a colony of [[common midwife toad|midwife toads]], also referred to as bell toads,{{cite web|url=http://mediafiles.thedms.co.uk/Publication/YK/cms/pdf/11-media-experience-Gardens%20and%20Green%20Spaces%202013.pdf |title=Yorks Gardens and Green spaces |website=www.visityork.org/media/factsheets/experienceyork.aspx |access-date=29 June 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180925025718/http://mediafiles.thedms.co.uk/Publication/YK/cms/pdf/11-media-experience-Gardens%20and%20Green%20Spaces%202013.pdf |archive-date=25 September 2018}}{{cite book|first=John |last=Armitage |title=The Naturalist |publisher=Yorkshire Naturalists' Union |year=1964 |chapter=Two English Midwife-Toad colonies|pages=[https://archive.org/details/naturalistyorksh1964york/page/65 65]-66|oclc=1047634622|url=https://archive.org/details/naturalistyorksh1964york|access-date=25 April 2019}} and it was once home to a number of exotic pets including [[axolotl]]s and green lizards which were introduced into the garden in the early 1930s.{{cite web|url=http://www.yorkpress.co.uk/news/10610474.Animal_sculptures_go_on_display_at_Goddards/ |title=Animal sculptures go on display at Goddards |website=[[The Press (York)|York Press]] |date=14 August 2013 |access-date=29 June 2016}} In 2016 the National Trust revealed plans to recreate the original planting schemes drawn up by Dillistone almost ninety years earlier.{{cite web|url=http://www.yorkshirepost.co.uk/news/historic-design-of-york-stately-home-s-gardens-to-be-recreated-90-years-on-1-8015405 |title=Historic design of York stately home's gardens to be recreated 90 years on |work=The Yorkshire Post |date=15 July 2016 |access-date=15 September 2016}} {{clear|left}} ===Carriage entrance=== [[File:Goddards, Tadcaster Road - geograph.org.uk - 1090175.jpg|thumb|left|The carriage entrance facing on to Tadcaster Road, Dringhouses|alt=A redbrick building with a road through the centre]] Brierley was also the architect for the Grade II* listed [[gatehouse]] at the entrance to Goddards, a red brick structure with staircase [[Turret (architecture)|turret]]s{{NHLE|num=1256505 |desc=No 25 including Carriage Entrance|accessdate=23 June 2016|fewer-links=yes}} which incorporates a flat roofed [[garage (residential)|motor house]]. {{cite journal |last= Smith |first= Pete |title= The Motor Car and the Country House: Historical Buildings Report |url= http://services.english-heritage.org.uk/ResearchReportsPdfs/094_2010WEB.pdf |journal= Research Department Report Series No.94-2010 |publisher= English Heritage |pages= 113 |issn= 1749-8775 |access-date= 27 June 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170202011819/http://services.english-heritage.org.uk/ResearchReportsPdfs/094_2010WEB.pdf |archive-date= 2 February 2017 |url-status= dead }} It was originally the home of the Terry's chauffeur{{cite book |last=Wilson |first=Van |date=2009 |title=The Story of Terry's |publisher=York Oral History Society |page=77 |isbn=978-0951365250}} and remains in residential use. ==The Terry Family at Goddards== Noel Terry (1889–1980) was the great-grandson of Joseph Terry, the first [[Terry's|Terry]] of the family confectionery business. Noel was brought up at Trentholme, the home of his maternal grandfather, located {{convert|0.8|mi|km}} north of Goddards, and opposite the Elmbank Hotel which, at the time, was the home of Sidney Leetham, an uncle of Kathleen Leetham (1892–1980).{{NHLE|num=1256439|desc=Elm Bank Hotel|accessdate=25 April 2019|fewer-links=yes}}{{cite web|url=https://houseandheritage.org/2015/11/30/goddards/ |title=Goddards |website=houseandheritage.org|date=30 November 2015|access-date=25 April 2019}} The Leetham family were owners of a large flour-milling business in the Hungate area of York.{{cite web|url=https://www.yorkarchaeology.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/YAT-17-web.pdf|title=Industrialisation in Hungate|work=Yorkshire Archaeology Today: Number 17, Autumn 2009|page=7|access-date=25 April 2019|archive-date=25 April 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190425152216/https://www.yorkarchaeology.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/YAT-17-web.pdf|url-status=dead}} Kathleen lived at Aldersyde, a large house that her father Henry Ernest Leetham commissioned in 1895 and which is located {{convert|0.5|mi|km|1}} south of Goddards.{{NHLE|num=1245577|desc=Aldersyde|accessdate=25 April 2019|fewer-links=yes}} In 1915, Noel's brother, [[J. E. Harold Terry]], married Kathleen's sister, [[Constance Leetham]]{{cite web|url=https://archive.org/details/whoswho1926001356mbp |title=Who's Who 1926 – p.2861 – Terry (Joseph Edward) Harold|website=archive.org |access-date=2 July 2016}} and Noel and Kathleen were also married having overcome the objections of her father who had initially opposed their relationship. Soon after the marriage Noel was sent to France due to the [[First World War]] and in 1916 was wounded at the [[Battle of the Somme]] whilst serving with the 5th [[West Yorkshire Regiment]]. After he returned home they started a family together and by 1925 had two sons, Peter and Kenneth, a daughter, Betty, and plans to move to a larger house. From 1927 Goddards would become the family home of the Terry's and their children – with their youngest son Richard being born the following year. The name of the house came from Noel Terry's middle name, which was that of his grandmother, Frances Goddard, first wife of [[Sir Joseph Terry]]. By the 1930s Noel had become a managing director at Terry's and it was at this time that the company introduced two of their most famous products – [[Terry's All Gold]] and the [[Terry's Chocolate Orange|Chocolate Orange]]. When production was interrupted by the [[Second World War]] Noel became a Controller with the [[Royal Observer Corps]] and was awarded an [[Order of the British Empire|MBE]] in 1943.{{London Gazette|issue=36035|date=28 May 1943|page=2498|supp=y}} His son Kenneth served in the RAF and was awarded the [[Distinguished Flying Cross (United Kingdom)|DFC]] in 1942. He died in 1944 and is commemorated on the local war memorial (also by Brierley).{{cite web|url=https://www.iwm.org.uk/memorials/item/memorial/30797|title=Memorial: Dringhouses|publisher=Imperial War Museum|access-date=25 April 2019}} Noel continued to work at Terry's until 1970, and his son Peter, who had joined Terry's in 1945, became deputy managing director. Although the house was built in the Arts and Crafts style it would become furnished with a large assortment of [[Georgian era|Georgian]] furniture and clocks which Noel Terry collected throughout his life. It is thought that his enthusiasm in antiques was partly inspired by his father-in-law who had been a collector of porcelain and jade. His interest in history also led to his involvement with [[York Civic Trust]], of which he was honorary treasurer for many years. After Noel and Kathleen died in 1980 Noel's collection was put on display at [[Fairfax House]], in York, a [[Georgian architecture|Georgian]] house museum renovated by the Civic Trust.{{cite web|url=http://www.fairfaxhouse.co.uk/fairfax-house/explore/noel-terry/ |title=Noel Terry & His Collection |website=www.fairfaxhouse.co.uk |access-date=27 June 2016}} ==National Trust era== [[File:Goddards York glasshouse.jpg|thumb|The [[greenhouse|glasshouse]] at Goddards was made by Richardson of Darlington and restored by the National Trust.{{cite web|url=https://www.yorkshiregardenstrust.org.uk/sites/yorkshiregardenstrust.org.uk/files/documents/YGT_newsletter_28.pdf |title=Historic Glasshouses |work=Newsletter: Issue 28, New Series 10, Winter 2011 |publisher=Yorkshire Gardens Trust |page=4 |access-date=24 April 2019}}|alt=A greenhouse, the bottom section is brick and the top half is a white wooden frame with glass panels.]] When the National Trust took over Goddards it was initially only for use as regional offices rather than a visitor attraction. However, the garden was opened to the public in 2006 and the house in 2012.{{cite web|url=http://www.yorkshirelife.co.uk/people/goddards_national_trust_opens_york_house_built_by_terry_s_chocolate_1_1571587 |title=Goddards – National Trust opens York house built by Terry's chocolate |work=Yorkshire Life |date=7 September 2012 |access-date=23 June 2016}} The rooms displayed period furniture used to recreate the atmosphere of the 1930s when the house was at its busiest and the family business at its zenith. As well as owning a chocolate factory Terry's also had its own tearoom and shop in York, whose cakes inspired the food served in the dining room at Goddards.{{cite web|url= http://www.yorkpress.co.uk/features/features/9828825.A_house_built_on_chocolate/ |title=A house built on chocolate |work=York Press|date=20 July 2012 |access-date=2 July 2016}} Exhibits at Goddards |author=Mike Laycock |access-date=16 September 2016}}{{cite web|url=http://www.yorkmix.com/things-to-do/how-york-chocolate-boss-used-to-live-pictures/ |title=How York chocolate boss used to live – pictures |work=YorkMix |date=24 July 2012 |access-date=16 September 2016}} In 2014 and 2015 Goddards was listed as a finalist in the 'Visitor Attraction of the Year (Under 50,000 Visitors)' category
